body:
# The canonical register: Kalki

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Kalki, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Kalki to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The name is attested as **कल्कि**, on the evidence Mahābhārata 3.191 (the earliest Kalki prophecy) and Kalki Purāṇa (the full biography) set down. On the evidence, it means "The avatāra yet to come — the tenth and final avatāra of Viṣṇu, who appears at the end of the Kali Yuga riding a white horse to destroy unrighteousness and restore the age of truth". The canonical transliteration is **Kalki**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “KAHL-kee” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *kalki* differs from the canonical *Kalki* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The Kalki cycle absorbed apocalyptic expectations from every quarter: the White Horse echoes the sun-horse of Indo-Iranian myth; the sword of the age borrows Paraśurāma’s axe; and Śambhala, his hidden kingdom, became the axis of Tibetan Buddhism’s Kalacakra — the wheel of time teachings centred on the king who will come.

And it never stopped working. Kalki is eschatology’s most durable prophetic figure in the living world: films, novels, and comics re-stage his coming endlessly, and ‘waiting for Kalki’ is an idiom for expecting the end of a corrupt order.  The Śambhala legend seeded Theosophy’s Shambhala and, through it, a century of Western occult geography.

## The Convention's Own History

Long before IAST was formalized in 1912, Sanskrit had Pāṇini — the fourth-century-BCE grammarian whose rules describe the language's sounds with a precision no other ancient tradition matched. That heritage is why the convention is so exact: retroflexes (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ) are not accented dentals but separate phonemes with separate meanings; long and short vowels (ā/a, ī/i, ū/u) change words, not just timing. IAST writes those distinctions down with underdots and macrons so that a reader who has never heard Sanskrit can still read it *correctly*. Dropping the marks is not transliteration at a lower resolution — it is a different, lesser claim.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Kalki** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Kalki** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *kalki* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Kalki** stands at [/kalki/](/kalki/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Mahābhārata 3.191 (the earliest Kalki prophecy), Kalki Purāṇa (the full biography), Bhaviṣya Purāṇa (the Kali Yuga lists).
